info.bio: Television es una banda estadounidense de rock que es considerada una de las más importantes de la primera ola del punk de Nueva York de mediados y fines de los años 70. A pesar de ser frecuentemente considerada como una banda de punk, Television tenía un estilo distintivo en el que las guitarras de Tom Verlaine y Richard Lloyd eran el centro de atención, por lo que han sido comparados con bandas de rock psicodélico como The Grateful Dead. Television fue la primera banda de rock que tocó en el famoso club CBGB

scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo

scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».

scenes.name: Nueva psicodelia y big music: Echo & the Bunnymen y U2
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En lugar de descender a lo oscuro, elevarse hacia la luz. Liverpool, que no tuvo punk clásico ni postpunk experimental, quería que la música fuera «una fiesta» (Bill Drummond, Zoo): el club Eric's, las bandas fantasma (The Crucial Three, Big in Japan), Wah! Heat, The Teardrop Explodes de Julian Cope. Echo & the Bunnymen, con el minimalismo aprendido de Television y la voz de Ian McCulloch, graban Crocodiles y Heaven Up Here, respuesta luminosa a Closer, y heredan el público huérfano de Joy Division; Ocean Rain los vuelve estrellas pop. U2, «punk positivo» cristiano y pacifista, guitarra de The Edge como sintetizador, quiere ocupar el lugar de Curtis: War (1983), «Sunday Bloody Sunday» en MTV, The Unforgettable Fire con Eno. Alrededor, la «big music» celta de Simple Minds, The Waterboys, Big Country y la neopsicodelia de The Blue Orchids.

scenes.name: New wave neoyorquina
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: 1976 es un año bisagra: los sellos independientes revitalizan la industria y nuevos géneros la escena, una revolución comparable a la de 1966. Los jóvenes de los setenta, sin sueños tras la derrota de la contracultura, canalizan su aburrimiento en un sonido crudo emparentado con el garage. Nueva York es la capital: el CBGB's y el Max's Kansas City. Patti Smith, Richard Hell (el profeta: «Blank Generation» y la ética punk), Television (Marquee Moon, que define la estética de la new wave), Tom Verlaine, y los Ramones, que tocan rock'n'roll inepto a velocidad supersónica e inventan el género más importante del último cuarto de siglo.

scenes.name: Space-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Tras la orgía de distorsión del dream-pop y el shoegazing, en EE UU se busca disciplina: Mark Kramer (Shockabilly, B.A.L.L., Bongwater, el coloso The Guilt Trip); los Flaming Lips, los discípulos más locos de Pink Floyd, entre la ética punk y el burlesque hippy (Oh My Gawd, Zaireeka); Red Temple Spirits, Viv Akauldren. Galaxie 500 y Yo La Tengo, los grupos que más influirán en la década siguiente: la psicodelia como estupor exangüe (Today, On Fire) y las baladas abstractas de texturas (May I Sing With Me). Y Phish, indiferentes a la estética punk, recuperan el directo, el solo de guitarra y la improvisación colectiva.

podcast.title: Pioneering Performances at CBGB (1973)
podcast.body: In December 1973, band members Richard Hell, Richard Lloyd, and Tom Verlaine approached Hilly Crystal, owner of a bar named CBGBOMFUG, and secured a Sunday night slot for their band, Television, to perform for an admission fee of $1. After a challenging beginning, their performances at CBGB, combined with the earlier collapse of the Mercer Art Center, helped establish the club as the epicenter for New York's burgeoning punk rock scene. "Marina Half Weeks later, television played their first ever rock night at CBGB. And admission was $1."

podcast.title: Tom Verlaine Death (January 28, 2023) – Prostate Cancer, Age 73; Helped CBGB Become Ground Zero for Punk
podcast.body: Tom Verlaine co-founded Television and in 1973 helped Hilly Kristal — owner of a scuzzy bar on Bleecker Street in a then-terrible part of New York — to let Television play a Sunday night residency. This decision catalyzed CBGB into becoming ground zero for New York punk and, by chain reaction, the entire international punk movement. Television produced two critically acclaimed albums before breaking up in 1978. Verlaine subsequently collaborated with Patti Smith, worked with James Iha of the Smashing Pumpkins, had a song covered by David Bowie, and was involved in a 1992 Television reunion album. He was scheduled to produce Jeff Buckley's second album — a project ended when Buckley drowned in the Mississippi River in 1997. Verlaine was diagnosed with prostate cancer at some point in the 2000s; it metastasized. He died January 28, 2023, age 73. "That was the catalyst for making CBGB ground zero for the world of New York punk."

podcast.body: Television's Sunday night residency quickly became one of the best nights at CBGB, drawing the crowd that had been displaced by the collapse of the Mercer Arts Center. This growing interest led Hilly Crystal to institute a rock-only policy within a few months of Television's debut, signifying the club's transformation into a hub for the new scene. podcast.title: Early Residency at CBGB
podcast.body: Television began playing a regular Sunday Night Residency at Hilly Crystal's bar, which would soon become widely known as CBGB. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

podcast.body: Television, led by Tom Verlaine, were pivotal in giving form to the nascent New York punk scene in the mid-1970s. Their angular guitar riffs, long yet minimalist songs, and urban poetic aesthetic stood in stark contrast to the prevailing hippism, helping to define a new direction for rock music. "Delevisión, liderados por Tom Verlain, fueron los primeros en darle forma a esa escena."

podcast.body: Verlaine, who had jazz roots, initially avoided the guitar, considering it a "wimpy instrument." His perspective changed after hearing The Yardbirds, particularly guitarists like Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, and Jeff Beck. Over time, he developed a unique style, even drawing inspiration from surf guitarists like Dick Dale to cultivate his sound. "Then hearing the yard birds changed that and I guess that would that would happen. Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Jeff Beck, hearing those guys will change your mind about the guitar."

The two-minute interview, which featured multiple instances of swearing on live television, including the word "f**k," immediately became a gigantic national scandal, leading to headlines condemning "punk rock scum" and "the filth in the fury." xref.title: Naked in Bed with Mick Jagger – Angela Bowie's 1990 TV Claim, Denied Then Partially Walked Back
xref.body: On May 4, 1990, David Bowie's ex-wife Angela appeared on the Joan Rivers Show, newly freed from a 10-year gag order after their divorce. She stated on national television: "I caught him in bed with Mick Jagger — and yes, they were naked." Bowie was a professed bisexual during the 1970s. Mick Jagger immediately dismissed the claim as "rubbish," and Bowie's lawyer sent an open letter stating that "any implication that there was ever a gay affair between Mick Jagger and David Bowie is an absolute fabrication." Within a week, Angela was qualifying her statement. By her 1993 autobiography, the account had evolved: she had walked in, assumed they had been having sex, and that was her honest belief, but she had no proof. An additional complication: Angela may have had her own affair with Jagger during the marriage, possibly inspiring the Rolling Stones song "Angie" — or, in another rumor, that "Angie" referred to David himself using a nickname. "Did they spend the night together? Yes. Were they naked? Apparently. Was it sexual? Who knows?"

xref.title: SNL Pope John Paul II Photo Tear (October 3, 1992) – Career-Ending Television Moment
xref.body: After a series of controversies (refusing to appear on SNL while Andrew Dice Clay was host in 1990; refusing the national anthem before a New Jersey show in August 1990; skipping the 1991 Grammys despite four nominations; a perceived pro-Saddam comment in March 1991), Sinead O'Connor appeared on *Saturday Night Live* on October 3, 1992, singing Bob Marley's "War." In rehearsal she held a picture of a refugee child; live, she substituted a photo of Pope John Paul II — taken from her mother's bedroom wall — and tore it up at the word "evil," saying "fight the real enemy." There was complete silence from the studio audience. NBC received nearly 5,000 complaints and the resulting media blowback permanently ended her mainstream career. The inspiration was Bob Geldof tearing up a picture of John Travolta on *Top of the Pops* in the 1970s. "NBC received almost 5,000 complaints.
